newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala names post-war truth commission.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala names post-war truth commission.

text.p: The United Nations named on Saturday a lawyer and a Mayan woman university professor to a three-person truth commission charged with investigating 36 years of war crimes in Guatemala.

"Working with me on the commission will be Otilia Lux, a pedagogy professor, and noted jurist Alfredo Balsells," Christian Tomuschat, a U.N. human rights expert designated two weeks ago to lead the commission, told a news conference.
Tomuschat oversaw the selection of Lux and Balsells to the commission, which will operate under the terms of peace accords signed Dec. 29 to end three decades of civil war.

Tomuschat, a German, monitored human rights in Guatemala for the U.N. in the early 1990s and impressed both sides of the conflict with his impartiality and his ability to master Spanish in a three-month crash course.
He said the commission, funded by international donations for Guatemala's peace process, will begin work in two months.
Unlike other so-called truth commissions in South Africa and Argentina, Guatemala will not name names of people responsible for war crimes, which critics say makes the commission's mandate worthless.
The government and leftist rebels, the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG), designed the truth commission during peace talks in 1994.
The commission will work for six months to a year, at the invitation of the government and the URNG.
According to the formula set out in the accord, a panel of university professors proposed Balsells for the commision.
Tomuschat chose Lux after conducting a series of interviews with human rights leaders, government officials and members of congress.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta Menchu and other prominent Guatemalans had pushed Tomuschat to select an Indian woman to sit on the commission.

During the brutal war, thousands of Guatemala's Mayan Indians were massacred and their villages became battlegrounds. Most of the foot soldiers in both the government and rebel armies were also poor Indians.
Guatemala earned one of the worst human rights records in the Americas when the army massacred civilians during a scorched-earth counterinsurgency campaign in the 1980s.

Under peace accords, the commission's mandate is to "objectively" report on all the violence and human rights violations on both sides of the war and recommend "measures to preserve the memory of the victims."
